title: S&P 500, Dow Close at Record Highs as AI Earnings and Iran Deal Hopes Converge
excerpt: Palantir surged nearly 30% and Caterpillar lifted the Dow by over 300 points, while a potential Iran deal drove oil down 5% and cooled rate-hike bets.
body:
• The S&P 500 gained 1.81% to close at 7,737.70, its first record since July 2, while the Dow rose 912 points to breach 54,000 for the first time.
  • Palantir soared nearly 30% after reporting 93% revenue growth and raising full-year guidance by $500 million; Caterpillar jumped on a 48% surge in power-generation sales tied to data-center demand.
  • Crude oil fell about 5% after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a deal with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could come within two days, cutting Fed rate-hike odds for September from 67.2% to 56.9%.
  • Of 304 S&P 500 companies that have reported Q2 earnings, 85.2% have beaten estimates, well above the long-term average of 67.5%.

The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed at fresh record highs on Tuesday, driven by a powerful combination of AI-fueled earnings beats and growing hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough in the Iran conflict that sent crude oil prices tumbling, according to Reuters.

The S&P 500 gained 137.20 points, or 1.81%, to finish at 7,737.70 — its first closing record since July 2. The Dow surged 912.25 points, or 1.72%, to 54,090.66, breaching the 54,000 milestone for the first time. The Nasdaq Composite rose 668.10 points, or 2.58%, to 26,581.99.

Palantir and Caterpillar Lead the Charge

Palantir Technologies soared nearly 30%, recording its biggest single-day percentage gain since February 2024. The data analytics firm reported 93% revenue growth in the latest quarter and raised its full-year revenue forecast by $500 million, according to Barron's.

Caterpillar, widely regarded as a bellwether for the global industrial economy, jumped after raising its annual revenue growth forecast. The company disclosed that power-generation sales surged 48% during the last three months, driven primarily by data-center construction demand. The stock accounted for more than 300 points of the Dow's gains on its own.

"I don't sense one ounce of skepticism among investors, from oil to interest rates to equities."

— Jack Ablin, Chief Investment Strategist, Cresset Capital Management

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index shot up nearly 7%, rising for a fourth straight session after a brutal 20.6% decline in July. The S&P 500 tech sector was the day's best-performing group, gaining 4.1%.

Oil Drops on Iran Deal Hopes

Crude prices fell about 5% after a Qatari official said efforts to secure a diplomatic resolution to the conflict were continuing. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters a deal with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could come "today or tomorrow," according to the Wall Street Journal.

The decline in oil prices had immediate knock-on effects. Fed rate-hike expectations for September dropped to 56.9% from 67.2% in the prior session, per CME FedWatch data. U.S. Treasury yields retreated in tandem.

The S&P 500 had pulled back from all-time highs in early June as tensions between Iran and the U.S. resurfaced and concerns about elevated valuations weighed on AI-related stocks through July. Tuesday's rally erased those losses.

Earnings Season Remains Robust

The broad-based rally extended beyond AI plays. Of the 304 S&P 500 companies that have reported second-quarter earnings as of last Friday, 85.2% have beaten estimates — well above the long-term average of 67.5%, according to LSEG data. Every major S&P sector showed profit growth.

McDonald's advanced despite reporting mixed results. Pfizer gained on upbeat quarterly numbers. SpaceX was set to release its first earnings report since going public after the closing bell.

"The earnings reports were certainly supportive, and that's great news, but I'm not sure a handful of earnings reports justifies new records in the S&P."

— Jack Ablin, Chief Investment Strategist, Cresset Capital Management

What's Next

Labor market data will be in focus for the rest of the week. Tuesday's JOLTS report showed 7.4 million job openings in June, slightly below May but up from 7.2 million a year ago, according to Barron's. The ratio of openings to unemployed workers held steady at 1.0 for the fourth straight month.

ADP's private employment report is due Wednesday, with economists forecasting 75,000 jobs added in July. The week culminates with Friday's Bureau of Labor Statistics payrolls report, where forecasts call for 100,000 jobs added and an unemployment rate steady at 4.2%.

Markets will also watch for any concrete developments in the Iran negotiations. A confirmed deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz would likely send oil prices lower still, with broad implications for inflation expectations and Fed policy.
nri_angle: The broad Wall Street rally and falling oil prices may benefit Indian diaspora investors with U.S. equity exposure and could ease inflation-driven cost pressures.
